newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian pensioners get money, hotline to president.
newsitem.headline: Russian pensioners get money, hotline to president.

text.p: Russia's long-suffering pensioners should finally receive months of delayed pensions in full on Tuesday -- and President Boris Yeltsin wants to know about it if they do not.

First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, who is also finance minister, said last week the government had repaid its debts to pensioners as part of a drive to resolve deep-seated social problems, gather taxes and cut the budget deficit.

But a free hotline, due to start working on the July 1 deadline for paying out trillions of roubles (billions of dollars) in delayed pensions, will allow pensioners all over Russia to alert the president to any problems or delays in clearing the backlog.
Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Sysuyev said on Monday feedback from the hotline would be gathered into reports to be presented to the president every two days until July 7.

"It will be possible to talk not with a machine recording your suffering, but with a human being who will talk with the pensioner," Sysuyev, sitting behind placards displaying the toll-free numbers, told a news conference.
"The information will be brought to the attention of the president of the Russian Federation who is personally controlling the situation."

It was not clear whether the phone numbers would work as well for pensioners in Russia's more remote regions as in relatively well-off Moscow. Further afield the telephone service is notoriously bad and many people do not even own a telephone.

But if Russia's drive to settle accounts with its elderly citizens is successful, Tuesday will be a red-letter day not only for pensioners but for the government itself, wrestling with a huge non-payments crisis in all sectors of the economy.

Tax collections in the first four months of the year were well below targets, partly a symptom of a cash-flow crisis in debt-stricken companies and partly a cause of the huge backlog in pensions as well as wages to workers on the federal payroll.

In many regions, teachers, doctors and soldiers, among others, have not been paid for months, and reports of hunger strikes, desertions and even suicides are common in places where the situation is especially desperate.

Yeltsin instructed Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Monday to settle accounts with the demoralised army by the end of August, which military officials say totals trillions, if not tens of trillions of roubles (several billion dollars).
But Sysuyev said the debt should be paid even earlier.

"I know that the task assigned was even tougher -- to pay it off not by the end of August but in the course of a month," Sysuyev said, adding the focus on paying off pension arrears had meant other groups had not received the same attention.
"I am convinced we will complete this task not least because the situation (in the army) is very serious."
He did not say how much money was owed to the army, and he gave no details of how the money would be raised.

The government is taking companies firmly to task on paying overdue taxes, offering a choice between coughing up the money, restructuring the debt or bankruptcy, a drive Sysuyev said played a major role in covering the pension arrears.

Natural gas producer Gazprom, which produces a third of the world's natural gas, paid off a whopping 14.5 trillion roubles ($2.52 billion) only last week and some companies are taking up the offer to restructure their debt.

But the government will have to keep up the pressure on tax payments, and ministers say future timely pension wage payments will hinge partly on success in cutting other spending, a move the parliament fiercely opposes.

The opposition-dominated State Duma lower house of parliament rejected last week the government's bill proposing a one-fifth cut in 1997 spending. But ministers say cuts will go ahead with or without the Duma.
--Christina Ling, Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520 ($=5,766 roubles)
